problem: Temporal-distance-prediction subgoal selection (GNM, ViNG, SPTM) needs robot-collected training data, which is scarce, and costs O(n) network passes per step in the number of candidate nodes. This forces sliding-window heuristics that can drift and lose the robot.
motivation: Subgoal selection in topological navigation is essentially image retrieval, so it can be cast as visual place recognition. Place recognition has millions of non-robot training images (e.g. SF-XL with 41M), and its embeddings are precomputable and searchable by fast nearest-neighbour matching. Cheap matching also makes Bayesian filtering over all map nodes feasible, improving temporal consistency.
key_idea: Replace temporal-distance subgoal selection with a place-recognition embedding retrieval model (CosPlace) plus a discrete Bayesian filter over map nodes, keeping GNM's waypoint policy for goal reaching.
insight: Place-recognition models trained on generic street-view data generalize better than robot-data-trained temporal distance models, even indoors (SR 0.61 vs 0.39 with the same window). The offline VPR benchmark shows GNM Recall@1 is about an order of magnitude below CosPlace-LR, e.g. 8.9 vs 71.8 on Pitts30k, so GNM is fragile to appearance and viewpoint change. The Bayesian filter adds about 10 SR points over the sliding window by keeping a full belief that cannot get lost and escapes repetitive-pattern traps.
method: Subgoal selection via place recognition: the observation and map images are embedded separately by f_enc; the best-matching map node is found by Euclidean nearest-neighbour search, and the next node along the route is the subgoal. Map descriptors are precomputed offline.

CosPlace-LR encoder: an EfficientNet-B0 backbone with GeM pooling and 512-d descriptors, trained from scratch with CosPlace classification loss on SF-XL (41.2M images) resized to 85x85, to match the 85x64 inputs used by GNM.

Discrete Bayesian filter (adapted from Xu et al.): the belief over map nodes is propagated with a uniform motion model (w_u=2, w_l=-1) and updated with the measurement exp(-λ1||z_t - z_s||). λ1 is set automatically per session. It is initialized from the first query, so it works in kidnapped-robot mode.
Sliding-window alternative: only nodes near the previous subgoal are considered, as in SPTM and GNM. It is initialized at the first node.
Goal-reaching policy: the frozen pretrained GNM waypoint model predicts 5 waypoints, followed open-loop by the robot's low-level controller; the loop runs at 5 Hz.
Offline evaluation: GNM is adapted to the VPR-Benchmark and compared with CosPlace-LR and full-resolution CosPlace using Recall@N within 25 m.

setting.backbone: CosPlace-LR (EfficientNet-B0 + GeM, trained from scratch) for subgoal selection; GNM waypoint policy (pretrained, frozen)
setting.training_data: CosPlace-LR trained on SF-XL (41.2M street-view images, resized to 85x85); the GNM policy uses the authors' released weights (54 h of navigation data)
setting.observation: monocular front-facing RGB from a 175° fish-eye camera, downsized to 85x64
setting.action_space: predicted waypoints (5 waypoints with position and heading) tracked by a robot-specific controller
setting.privileged: none (a topological map from a prior manual reference run is required)

numbers_note: No standard simulator benchmarks; the results are real-robot success rates over 60 repetitions per setting, with SR printed as fractions (0-1). Runtimes: PlaceNav 19 ms (window) / 41 ms (Bayesian) vs GNM 45 ms (window 5) / 174 ms (window 21). The offline VPR Recall@1 is in Table 3 (e.g. CosPlace-LR Pitts30k 71.8 vs GNM 8.9).
results: PlaceNav with the Bayesian filter reaches an indoor SR of 0.69 vs 0.39 for GNM, and an outdoor SR of 0.58 vs 0.47, with lower runtime (19-41 ms vs 45-174 ms). The abstract reports 76% and 23% relative improvements respectively. On the offline VPR benchmark, CosPlace-LR beats GNM by roughly an order of magnitude in Recall@1.
limitations: Evaluated only on routes chosen to avoid waypoint-estimation failures and under limited illumination differences; the outdoor gain is smaller because waypoint estimation noise dominates.
Place recognition struggles with visually repetitive (bursty) content, and low-resolution 85x64 inputs sharply reduce recall; small sample sizes (60 runs per setting) with no statistical tests.
Requires a prior manual reference run to build the map; the goal-reaching policy is unchanged and not improved.
builds_on: Xu et al. probabilistic Bayesian filter for place recognition
